# Project Organization

Before we write a single line of R code, it's worth thinking about how your
project is organized. A well-organized project is easier to navigate, easier
to share, and easier to return to months later when you've forgotten exactly
what you did. This chapter covers some foundational habits for structuring a
reproducible data project, and introduces the final project you'll build
throughout the semester.

## Directory structure

A reproducible project keeps different kinds of files separated into clearly
labeled folders, rather than dumping everything into one location. A typical
structure looks something like this:

```
my_project/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/            # original, unedited data — never modify these files
│   └── processed/      # cleaned data produced by your scripts
├── scripts/            # R scripts and RMarkdown files
├── output/
│   ├── figures/        # plots and visualizations
│   └── tables/         # summary tables, model outputs
├── docs/               # notes, README files, other documentation
└── manuscript_files/   # finalized manuscript files for submission
```

The exact folder names and structure are less important than the underlying
principle: someone unfamiliar with your project — including future you —
should be able to look at the folder layout and understand what's in it and
how it's used.

## Golden rules

A few habits will save you a lot of pain down the road:

- **Never edit raw data by hand.** Once your original data file is in `data/raw/`,
  treat it as read-only. Any cleaning or transformation should happen in a
  script, so there's a record of exactly what changed and why.
- **Scripts should run top to bottom without manual intervention.** If your
  script depends on you clicking things in a specific order that isn't written
  down, it's not reproducible.
- **Use relative paths, not absolute paths.** A path like `data/raw/survey.csv`
  will work on any computer; a path like `/Users/yourname/Desktop/project/data/raw/survey.csv`
  will only work on yours.
- **Document as you go.** A future collaborator — or you, in six months — should
  be able to understand your project without asking you questions. This means
  annotating your code, and keeping your README files up date.

## Naming files

Good file names are both human-readable and computer-readable:

- Use lowercase letters, numbers, hyphens, or underscores — avoid spaces and
  special characters, which can cause problems in scripts and command lines.
- Be descriptive: `bird-counts-2023.csv` is more useful than `data1.csv`.
- If files need to sort in a meaningful order, use leading zeros:
  `01-clean-data.R`, `02-explore-data.R`, `03-make-figures.R` will sort
  correctly, while `1-clean-data.R`, `10-make-figures.R`, `2-explore-data.R`
  will not.

## Final Project: Topic and Dataset Selection

Throughout the semester, you'll apply the tools and concepts from this course
to a dataset of your own choosing. You'll select your topic and dataset now,
in Week 1, and build on it week by week as we introduce new skills — by the
end of the course, you'll have cleaned, explored, and visualized your dataset
using a fully reproducible workflow.

### Dataset eligibility criteria

Your dataset should have at least **100 rows (observations)** and **10 columns
  (variables)**. This ensures there's enough structure and complexity to
  meaningfully practice data wrangling and visualization.


### What to submit

Go to Canvas, and complete the "Week 1" assignment.

1. A brief description of your dataset, including an overview of how the data 
  were collected, how many observations there are, and how many variables were
  measured.
2. A short written explanation (3–5 sentences) of why this
  dataset interests you and what you hope to learn from it.
3. At least 2–3 questions you want to answer using
  this dataset by the end of the course.
4. A brief description on any data cleaning you anticipate needing to do, based 
  on an initial look at the file.
